title: Crane and Rigging Checks on Steel Jobs
summary: Cranes and rigging move every piece of steel. This talk covers the pre-shift inspection and rigging rules in Subpart R.
talking_points: Cranes used in steel erection must be visually inspected before each shift by a competent person, including observation for deficiencies during operation (29 CFR 1926.753(c)(1)(i)). Subpart CC also applies to hoisting and rigging (1926.753(a)).

The inspection includes control mechanisms, wear and contamination, safety devices such as boom angle indicators, boom stops and anti-two block devices, pressurized lines, hooks and latches, wire rope reeving, the hydraulic fluid level, tires, level position, and ground conditions including settling around outriggers (1926.753(c)(1)(i)(A)-(L)).
If a deficiency is found, a competent person must decide right away whether it is a hazard. A hazardous deficiency means the crane comes out of service until corrected (1926.753(c)(1)(ii)-(iii)).
The operator is responsible for operations under direct control and has the authority to stop and refuse to handle loads until safety is assured (1926.753(c)(1)(iv)).
A qualified rigger must inspect the rigging before each shift (1926.753(c)(2)).
The headache ball, hook or load must not be used to carry people. A crane or derrick may hoist employees only on a personnel platform meeting the Subpart CC rules (1926.753(c)(3)-(4)).

Safety latches on hooks must not be deactivated or made inoperable, except where a qualified rigger has determined that placing purlins and single joists is safer that way, or where equivalent protection is in a site-specific erection plan (1926.753(c)(5)).
site_hazards_to_check: Soft or sloping ground under outriggers
Damaged hooks, latches or wire rope
Safety devices bypassed or not working
Anyone riding the load or hook
discussion_questions: Who is the competent person who inspects the crane each shift?
When can the operator stop the lift, and who backs that up?
